title: Terrace and Balcony Gardens: What to Check Before You Plant
metaTitle: Terrace & Balcony Gardens: What to Check | Laavin
description: Before a terrace or balcony garden: check structure, waterproofing and drainage, use a lightweight mix and choose plants for Delhi heat.
lead: A terrace garden can cool the floor below, give people a place to sit and turn a hot, empty roof into the best space in the building. It can also leak, overload the slab or die in its first summer. The difference is almost always decided before a single plant goes in.
imageAlt: Young plants growing under a fine irrigation mist
body:
1. Start with the structure

Wet soil is heavy, and a roof slab was usually designed for people and water tanks, not for a garden. Before anything else, have a structural engineer confirm how much load the terrace can safely carry. Plan heavier elements, such as deep planters, trees and water features, over beams and columns rather than in the middle of a span.

2. Fix the waterproofing first

Most terrace garden problems are really waterproofing problems. Inspect the existing membrane, repair or replace it, and add a root barrier so roots cannot work their way into joints. A protection layer over the membrane stops it being punctured during installation.

Then test it. A simple ponding test, where the roof is flooded and checked for leaks over a day or two, is far cheaper than lifting a finished garden to find a leak.

Waterproofing is the one part of a terrace garden you cannot easily redo later. Get it right, and test it, before you plant.

3. Plan the drainage

Water must leave the roof quickly, especially in the monsoon. The usual build-up is a drainage layer over the waterproofing, a filter fabric to keep soil out of it, and then the growing medium. The roof should slope towards outlets, and every outlet should stay reachable for cleaning.

4. Use a lightweight growing mix

Ordinary garden soil is too heavy and compacts in containers. Terrace gardens use a lighter mix, typically built from cocopeat, compost and a mineral such as perlite or vermiculite, which holds water without becoming waterlogged. Depth depends on what you plant: lawns and ground covers need the least, shrubs need more, and small trees need the deepest beds or large planters.

5. Choose plants for heat and wind

A Delhi rooftop is hotter, windier and brighter than the ground below. Plants that cope well include bougainvillea, frangipani, hibiscus, tecoma, ornamental grasses and many succulents. Herbs such as lemongrass and tulsi do well in containers. Keep tall or top-heavy plants away from the edges, and anchor large planters against wind.

  • Full sun and wind: bougainvillea, ornamental grasses, succulents.
  • Flowering colour: hibiscus, tecoma, frangipani in larger planters.
  • Shade and screening: pergolas with climbers rather than heavy trees.

6. Water with drip, on a timer

Rooftop plants dry out fast in May and June and need far less water in winter. A drip system on a timer, with a separate line for any lawn, delivers water at the roots and can be adjusted by season. It also keeps water off the waterproofing where it is not needed.

7. Look after it

Clear every outlet before the monsoon, trim plants that catch the wind, top up the growing mix as it settles, and feed regularly, because containers hold fewer nutrients than open ground.

8. Balconies follow the same rules

A balcony garden is a terrace garden in miniature. Check what the slab can carry, raise planters on feet or trays so water can drain off the floor, use the same lightweight mix, and choose plants for the light the balcony actually gets. Railing planters must be fixed securely, especially on higher floors.

How we approach terrace and balcony gardens

On our team, the structure, waterproofing and drainage are checked by a civil and electrical engineer retired from the Delhi Development Authority, and the plants and growing mix are chosen by a horticulturist with an M.Sc. in Botany. See our landscape services.

proof.text: Structure, waterproofing and drainage checked before planting begins.

title: Planning a Farmhouse Garden for the Delhi NCR Climate
metaTitle: Farmhouse Garden Planning in Delhi NCR | Laavin
description: Planning a farmhouse garden in Delhi NCR: test the soil, plan the water, plant windbreaks and shade, choose a hardy lawn, time it right.
lead: A farmhouse gives you space that a city home never does: room for lawns, an orchard, shade trees and a kitchen garden. It also brings the full force of the NCR climate, from hot dry winds in May to heavy monsoon rain and cold winter nights. A good farmhouse garden is planned around all of it.
imageAlt: Landscaped courtyard with a pergola, lawn and evening lighting
body:
1. Plan the zones before you plant

Walk the plot and divide it into zones: the arrival and driveway, the lawn around the house, an orchard, a kitchen garden, and a service area for water tanks, pumps and storage. Deciding this first stops you planting a tree where a driveway or a pipe needs to go later.

2. Test the soil

Soil across NCR varies a lot, and some areas have alkaline or salty patches that hold plants back. A basic soil test for pH, salinity and organic matter tells you what to correct and which plants will do well. It costs very little compared with replacing plants that never establish.

3. Sort out the water

Know where your water comes from, how much you have and how good it is. Check the local rules on groundwater use, and plan rainwater harvesting so that monsoon water recharges the ground instead of running off. Lay out the main pipelines before planting, so you are not digging up a new lawn later.

On a farmhouse, water decides almost everything else. Plan it first, and the garden becomes far easier to keep alive.

4. Plant windbreaks and shade trees early

Trees take the longest to grow, so plant them first. A row of trees along the boundary that faces the hot summer winds protects everything inside it. Native and naturalised trees such as neem, arjun, jamun and pilkhan cope with the heat, give dense shade and need little care once established.

5. Choose a lawn that can take the heat

Doob grass, a Bermuda type, handles north Indian summers and heavy use well. Keep large lawns where you will actually use them, and use ground covers or mulched beds in the rest. That saves a great deal of water and mowing.

6. Add an orchard and kitchen garden

Mango, guava, citrus, pomegranate, amla and jamun all grow well in the region. Plant them in well-prepared pits with compost, protect young trees from animals, and give each one enough room to reach full size. A small kitchen garden near the house, with raised beds and drip lines, keeps fresh herbs and vegetables within easy reach.

7. Time planting with the seasons

  • Monsoon, July to September: the best time for most trees and shrubs.
  • February and March: a good second window before the heat.
  • May and June: avoid new planting; focus on watering what is already in the ground.

8. Water with drip and sprinklers

Use drip lines for trees, beds and the orchard, and sprinklers only for the lawn. Split the system into zones by water need and run it on timers, so each area gets what it needs without waste.

How we approach farmhouse gardens

Our horticulturist, who holds an M.Sc. in Botany and has 30+ years of field experience, chooses species for your soil and the season, and the same team designs and installs the irrigation. See our landscape services and irrigation services.

title: Landscaping for Hotels and Resorts: A Practical Guide
metaTitle: Hotel & Resort Landscaping Guide | Laavin Infrascapes
description: Landscaping a hotel or resort: plan the guest journey, plant arrival courts and pool decks, build event lawns that recover, and upkeep.
lead: In a hotel, the landscape is part of the product. Guests judge the property by the arrival court before they reach the lobby, photograph the pool deck and remember the lawn where the wedding was held. Unlike most landscapes, it has to look its best every single day.
imageAlt: Courtyard with a water channel, palms and flowering trees
body:
1. Design around the guest journey

Follow the path a guest takes: the gate, the driveway, the arrival court, the lobby, the rooms, the pool, the restaurants and the event spaces. Each stop needs a different kind of landscape, and the moments guests notice most deserve the most care.

2. Make the arrival court count

The arrival court sets the first impression. Use bold, simple planting that reads well from a moving car, a focal point such as a tree, sculpture or water feature, and lighting that makes it just as striking at night. Choose plants that stay tidy all year rather than ones that look spectacular for a few weeks.

3. Plant pool decks with care

Around pools, avoid thorny plants and trees that drop heavy leaves, fruit or flowers into the water. Give loungers real shade, keep roots well away from the pool shell and paving, and use planting to screen service areas and neighbouring buildings.

A hotel landscape is judged on its worst day, not its best. Choose plants and layouts that stay neat with routine care.

4. Build event lawns that recover

Wedding and event lawns take heavy footfall, stages and marquees. They need a hard-wearing grass, good sub-surface drainage so they dry quickly after rain, and a maintenance plan that includes rest, aeration and repair between events.

5. Bring green indoors and onto terraces

Green walls and large planters soften lobbies, corridors and restaurant terraces. They need built-in irrigation, the right light, and plants chosen for indoor or partly shaded conditions.

6. Light it for the evening

Many guests see the grounds mostly after dark. Warm uplighting on trees, low path lights and underwater lights in water features extend the landscape into the evening and make the property feel safe and welcoming.

7. Water efficiently

Drip irrigation for beds and planters and zoned sprinklers for lawns keep water use under control. Where treated water from the property is available for irrigation, check its quality before using it on sensitive plants.

8. Maintain without disturbing guests

  • Schedule mowing, pruning and spraying for early mornings or low-occupancy days.
  • Use quieter equipment near rooms and dining areas.
  • Plan seasonal colour changes ahead of peak periods and major events.

How we approach hotel grounds

One team designs the planting, irrigation, hardscape and lighting and then maintains them, so nothing falls between contractors. Water features and lighting are overseen by our engineer, who spent 30+ years with the Delhi Development Authority. See our landscape services and hardscaping services.

cta.text: Share the property location, a site plan or a few photos, and the spaces you want to improve. We will reply within 24 hours with ideas and an estimate.

title: Vertical Gardens and Green Walls: How to Keep Them Alive
metaTitle: Vertical Gardens & Green Walls Guide | Laavin
description: How vertical gardens work: choosing a system, protecting the wall, irrigation and light, plants for indoor and outdoor walls, and upkeep.
lead: A green wall can turn a bare facade, a lobby or a boundary wall into the most memorable part of a building. It is also one of the easiest landscapes to get wrong. A vertical garden has very little soil and no room for error, so it lives or dies by its system, its water and its light.
imageAlt: Lush trailing plants and greenery in a bright room
body:
1. Choose the right system

There are a few common ways to build a vertical garden, and each suits a different site and budget:

  • Modular panels or trays: plants grow in pre-planted units that clip onto a frame. Easy to replace one section at a time.
  • Felt or pocket systems: plants sit in fabric pockets fixed to a waterproof backing. Light and flexible, but they need very reliable watering.
  • Green facades: climbers grow up wires or a trellis from planters at the base. The simplest and lowest-maintenance option for large outdoor walls, though slower to fill in.

2. Protect the wall behind it

A green wall keeps a lot of moisture against a building. The system should stand slightly off the wall on a frame, with a waterproof backing between the plants and the structure, so water never soaks into plaster or brickwork. The frame and fixings need to carry the full wet weight of the panels.

3. Irrigation is not optional

With so little growing medium, a vertical garden dries out within days if watering fails. It needs drip irrigation on a timer, emitters spread so every part of the wall gets water, and a gutter or tray at the base to catch the runoff. On larger walls, splitting the system into zones helps, because the top dries faster than the bottom.

Most failed green walls die of water problems: a blocked emitter, a timer that stopped, or a dry patch nobody noticed. Plan the irrigation as carefully as the planting.

4. Match the plants to the light

Light decides which plants will survive. Outdoor walls in full Delhi sun need hardy, heat-tolerant species, while shaded walls can take ferns and foliage plants. Indoors, most walls are darker than they look, so choose plants that tolerate low light, such as money plant, philodendron, syngonium and peace lily, or add grow lights where daylight is weak.

5. Think about the weather

Outdoor walls face hot dry winds in May and June and heavy rain in the monsoon. Plan for more frequent watering in summer, check that drainage copes with downpours, and avoid placing tender plants on the most exposed sides.

6. Plan the upkeep

  • Trim plants regularly so the wall stays even and nothing smothers its neighbours.
  • Check emitters and the timer often, and clean filters so lines do not clog.
  • Feed through the irrigation or by hand, because the medium holds few nutrients.
  • Replace weak plants quickly, before gaps spread.

How we approach vertical gardens

Our engineer checks the wall, the frame and the waterproofing, our horticulturist chooses plants for the light and exposure, and the same team installs and maintains the drip irrigation. See our landscape services.

cta.text: Send us a photo of the wall, its rough size and whether it is indoors or outdoors. We will reply within 24 hours with ideas and an estimate.

proof.text: Every green wall is planned with irrigation, drainage and waterproofing from the start.

title: Balcony Gardens: A Practical Guide for Apartments
metaTitle: Balcony Gardens for Apartments | Laavin Infrascapes
description: Planning an apartment balcony garden: read the light, respect weight and drainage, pick containers and plants, and water simply.
lead: A balcony is often the only outdoor space an apartment has, and a few well-chosen plants can make it the favourite spot in the home. Balconies are small, exposed and shared with neighbours below, so a good balcony garden is planned around light, weight and water from the start.
imageAlt: Potting soil, a trowel and young plants ready for containers
body:
1. Read the light first

The direction a balcony faces decides what will grow. An east-facing balcony gets gentle morning sun, a north-facing one stays bright but mostly shaded, and south and west faces get strong afternoon heat in a Delhi summer. Watch your balcony for a day and note how many hours of direct sun it gets before choosing plants.

2. Respect the weight and the floor

Wet soil and large pots are heavier than they look. Keep the heaviest containers near the wall or the edge supported by the building, not in the middle of a cantilevered slab. Raise pots on feet or trays so water can drain and the balcony floor stays dry, and check your society's rules before fixing anything to walls or railings.

3. Make sure water drains the right way

Water dripping onto the balcony below is the fastest way to upset a neighbour. Use pots with drainage holes, sit them in saucers or trays, and make sure the balcony floor drains to its outlet rather than over the edge.

On a balcony, the best garden is one your neighbours never notice: no drips, no falling pots, no leaves blowing onto the floor below.

4. Pick the right containers

Lighter containers, such as good-quality plastic, fibreglass or lightweight composite, keep the load down. Fill them with a light potting mix rather than garden soil. Railing planters should be fixed securely, especially on higher floors where the wind is stronger.

5. Choose plants for your light

  • Full sun: bougainvillea, hibiscus, succulents, and herbs such as tulsi and lemongrass.
  • Part sun: money plant, spider plant, syngonium and many flowering annuals in winter.
  • Shade: ferns, peace lily and other foliage plants that prefer softer light.

6. Keep watering simple

Small pots dry out quickly in summer and need far less water in winter. A small drip kit on a timer, or self-watering pots, keeps plants healthy when you travel and stops the overwatering that rots roots.

7. Plan for wind and birds

Higher floors catch more wind, so choose sturdy, low plants for exposed balconies and avoid tall pots near the railing. Pigeons are a common problem in many apartment blocks; bird netting keeps the garden and the floor clean.

How we approach balcony gardens

We check the weight, drainage and fixings, choose plants for the light your balcony actually gets, and can install a compact drip system so the garden looks after itself. See our landscape services.

title: How Mature Trees Are Transplanted on Highway Projects
metaTitle: How Mature Trees Are Transplanted on Highways | Laavin
description: How mature trees are moved out of road-widening corridors and kept alive: species, timing, root-ball preparation, replanting and aftercare.
lead: When a road is widened, mature trees are often in the way. Cutting them down is quick, but the city loses decades of shade, and projects often face delays and public objections. Moving the trees solves this: the road gets built and the trees live on nearby. Here is how it works, and what decides whether a moved tree survives.
imageAlt: A large mature tree with wide spreading branches
body:
Which trees can be moved?

Not every tree can be moved. First we survey each tree and note its type, trunk size, health and whether machines can reach it. Fig trees such as peepal, banyan and pilkhan usually recover well. Trees with a deep main root, and trees that are sick, hollow or leaning, are harder to move. We also check the new site. It needs space, good soil and a water supply.

When is the best time to move a tree?

In north India, the monsoon is usually the best time. The air is humid, so the tree loses less water while its roots recover. Peak summer is the worst time. Work starts weeks before the move. We water the tree deeply and cut back its branches, so there are fewer leaves to feed. We also cut the roots around the future root ball in stages, so the tree grows new small roots inside it.

How is a big tree dug out and lifted?

The root ball is sized to the trunk. The bigger the tree, the bigger and heavier the ball. We dig it out carefully, wrap it in hessian cloth and tie it, so the soil stays tight around the roots. Cranes and earth-movers then lift the tree onto a trailer. The aim is to keep the root ball whole and to replant the tree as fast as possible, ideally on the same day.

Plan tree moving into your construction schedule early. The survey and root work take weeks, and the best season may not match your earthwork dates.

How is the tree replanted?

We dig the new pit wider than the root ball, with good drainage and better soil. The tree goes in at the same depth and, where possible, facing the same way as before. Then we tie it with wires or stakes, so the wind cannot rock it while new roots grow.

What decides whether the tree survives?

Most of the work happens after the move. For the first year, the tree needs regular watering, root treatment, protection from fungus and pests, and regular checks. New leaves are the first sign that it has taken. Survival is also a contract issue. For example, Delhi's 2020 tree transplantation policy says at least 80% of moved trees must survive.

Our work on NH-307

On the NH-307 road-widening project, Laavin Infrascapes moved 155 mature roadside trees for NHAI. We followed the steps above and worked around the road contractor's schedule.

title: Carbon Sequestration Through Avenue and Median Plantation
metaTitle: Carbon Sequestration by Avenue Plantation | Laavin
description: How avenue and median plantation sequesters carbon, how to estimate it, which species suit north India, and why survival matters most.
lead: Every highway project in India now includes planting. Under the Green Highways Policy 2015, the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways sets aside 1% of highway project costs for planting and upkeep. When it is done well, roadside trees take carbon out of the air for decades. When it is done badly, the plants die within two summers and store almost nothing.
imageAlt: A road running under a canopy of tall avenue trees
body:
How do trees store carbon?

Trees take in carbon dioxide (CO₂) as they grow. They lock the carbon into their wood, roots and leaves. About half of a tree's dry weight is carbon. Every tonne of stored carbon equals about 3.67 tonnes of CO₂ taken out of the air. So the carbon a plantation stores depends mainly on how much wood it grows. That depends on the type of tree, how fast it grows and how long it lives, and most of all on whether it survives.

Do roadside trees and median shrubs store the same carbon?

No. The rows of trees along the edges of a road (avenue trees) do most of the carbon work. A large tree that lives long keeps adding wood for decades. Medians are different. They are usually planted with shrubs kept low, to block headlight glare without hiding traffic. So they hold little wood. Medians still matter, but mostly for other reasons.

  • Avenue rows: large, long-lived trees. They store the most carbon and give shade to people walking and cycling.
  • Medians: thick, low shrubs. They store a little carbon. Their main jobs are cutting glare, catching dust and looking good.
  • Green belts beside the road: several rows of tall trees and shrubs, where there is land. They store carbon and screen the road.

Which trees work best in north India?

For avenue rows, local trees that handle heat, dust and dry spells do best. Neem, peepal, pilkhan, arjun, jamun, amaltas and kachnar are common choices. Peepal and pilkhan grow large and live long, so they store a lot of carbon. For medians, hardy shrubs such as kaner (oleander) and bougainvillea are widely used. They cope with pollution, heat and little water.

Plant a mix of trees, not one type along the whole road. Then one pest or disease cannot wipe out the plantation. Spacing follows the project rules and road safety rules. Trees must not block the view at junctions or crowd cables and pipes.

How do you measure the carbon a plantation stores?

Good estimates come from measuring trees, not from rough figures per tree. The usual method is:

  1. Measure each tree's trunk width at chest height (1.3 m) and, if possible, its height.
  2. Use a published formula for that type of tree to estimate the dry weight above the ground.
  3. Add the weight of the roots, usually taken as a share of the weight above ground.
  4. Multiply the total dry weight by about 0.47 (the standard IPCC figure) to get the stored carbon.
  5. Multiply the carbon by 3.67 to show it as CO₂.

Repeat the measurements every year or two. The difference is the carbon stored in that time. Be careful with headline figures like "kilograms per tree per year". Young roadside trees store very little in their first years, and real numbers vary a lot by tree and site.

A dead sapling stores no carbon. On most roadside plantations, keeping plants alive matters more than how many you plant.

What keeps roadside plants alive?

Roadside plants face heat, dust, damage from vehicles, grazing animals and uneven watering. The plantations that survive usually have these things in common:

  • Bigger saplings that have been hardened in a nursery, not small seedlings.
  • Tree guards to protect them from animals and vehicles.
  • Regular watering through the first two or three summers, ideally with drip lines.
  • Quick replacement of dead plants, written into the maintenance contract.
  • Moving mature trees instead of cutting them down when a road is widened. A large tree already holds decades of stored carbon that a new sapling would take decades to replace.

Can a plantation earn carbon credits?

Yes, under international standards such as Verra's Verified Carbon Standard or the Gold Standard. But credits need a starting study, long-term monitoring and checks by an outside body. So they usually suit only large projects, or many projects grouped together. In India, the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change started the Green Credit Programme in 2023, and tree planting is one of the activities it covers. If you want credits, plan the monitoring from day one.

Our work

We planted 3,500 hardy plants that cope with pollution on the NH-7 median for an NHAI contractor. On NH-307 we moved 155 mature trees instead of cutting them down during road widening. See our planting and tree moving services.

title: Landscaping for Office Premises: A Practical Guide
metaTitle: Office Landscaping: A Practical Guide | Laavin Infrascapes
description: Landscaping office premises in India: shade, plant choice, water-efficient irrigation, terrace gardens, green building credits and upkeep.
lead: An office garden is the first thing visitors see, and one of the few places staff choose to spend time outside. It also costs money every month to water and maintain. Good office landscaping does both jobs: it creates spaces people use, with plants and systems that are affordable to keep alive.
imageAlt: Office courtyard with water channel, seating and palms
body:
Where should an office spend on landscaping?

Spend where people are. Walk the site with your facility team and note where people move and stop: the entrance and drop-off, walkways between buildings, parking, break areas, spots where people take calls or eat lunch, and the views from desks and meeting rooms. Put the best landscaping there. Quiet edges and service areas can stay simple and cheap to maintain.

Why does shade come first?

In an Indian summer, shade is what people want most from an outdoor space. Plant shade trees over parking, along walkways and around seating. Trees take years to grow, so use pergolas and shade structures in the meantime.

How should you choose the plants?

  • Choose local plants that suit the site. They need less water, fewer chemicals and fewer replacements.
  • Group plants by how much water they need, so thirsty plants and dry-loving plants are not watered on the same schedule.
  • Keep lawns only where people use them. Lawns need the most water. Use ground cover and shrub beds elsewhere.
  • Plan for the full-grown size, so trees do not crowd buildings, hide signs or lift paving in five years.

How can you cut the water bill?

Water is the biggest running cost. Use drip irrigation for shrub beds, hedges and trees, and sprinklers on timers for lawns. If the campus has a sewage treatment plant (STP), its treated water can often be used for watering, with proper filters. Rainwater harvesting and recharge pits reduce runoff and refill groundwater. Our guide to drip irrigation for large campuses explains where each system works best.

Can an office have a terrace garden or green wall?

Yes. A terrace garden can turn an empty roof into a break-out space. It needs proper waterproofing, a root barrier, a drainage layer and light soil. Your structural engineer should confirm the roof can carry the weight before design starts. Green walls look striking in lobbies and on outside walls. But they need built-in watering and regular care, so plan a maintenance budget from the start.

Does landscaping help with green building ratings?

It can. Landscaping can earn points in green building ratings such as IGBC and GRIHA. Native planting, smaller lawns, efficient watering and shade over paved areas all count. If your building is going for a rating, bring in the landscape contractor early, so the design supports the points you want.

A design your team cannot maintain will start to fail within a year. Agree on maintenance at the design stage, not after handover.

Who looks after the garden after handover?

Decide this early. Every landscape needs regular pruning, mowing, feeding, pest control and irrigation checks. Agree who does what, how often, and how dead plants are replaced. A simple monthly report with photos keeps everyone on track.

Checklist for facility managers

  • A site plan and photos of how the site looks now.
  • Where people walk, park, sit and gather.
  • Your water source and its quality: city supply, borewell or treated STP water.
  • Roof load and waterproofing details, if terraces are included.
  • Any green building rating you are aiming for.
  • A budget for building the garden and for the first year of maintenance.

See our office and commercial landscaping services.

title: Industrial Green Belts: Meeting Environmental Clearance Conditions
metaTitle: Industrial Green Belts and EC Conditions | Laavin
description: Planning an industrial green belt that meets environmental clearance conditions: area, density, species, fuel-site safety and records.
lead: Most factories that need an environmental clearance, or consent from a state pollution control board, must plant a green belt. This is a band of thick planting around the site that traps dust, cuts noise and screens the plant from neighbours. Inspectors check it. A green belt that exists on paper but not on the ground can become a compliance problem.
imageAlt: A dense belt of trees on both sides of a path
body:
What do green belt conditions usually ask for?

Every project has its own conditions, so first read your own clearance and consent orders. Common requirements include:

  • A green belt covering about a third (33%) of the plot.
  • About 2,500 trees per hectare.
  • Native trees, planted in several rows along the boundary.
  • Survival records and regular compliance reports.

How should a green belt be laid out?

A good green belt has layers. Tall trees go in the outer rows, medium trees in the middle and thick shrubs on the inside. Together they make a solid screen from the ground to the treetops. Put the thickest planting between the main sources of dust or smoke and the nearest neighbours, keeping the usual wind direction in mind. Leave routes open for fire engines, maintenance vehicles and inspections.

Which trees work best?

Choose trees that handle dust and pollution, stay green all year and have leaves that hold dust well. Rough or hairy leaves trap more dust. Neem, peepal, arjun, jamun and false ashoka are common choices in north India. Bamboo can make a quick screen while slower trees grow. Mixing trees protects the belt from one pest or disease.

What about fuel depots and other high-risk sites?

At fuel depots, chemical plants and other high-risk sites, safety rules limit what can be planted near storage tanks, pipelines and process areas. The green belt must keep clear zones clear, avoid piles of dry leaves and keep firebreaks open. Work with the site safety team from the start, and plan the belt around the safety layout, not the other way round.

At the Delhi Airport fuel facility, we built a green belt and landscape planned around the site's safety rules.

How do you get trees to survive on factory land?

Factory plots often have hard, filled-in or poor soil. Trees survive when you dig big pits with good soil and compost, water them reliably, protect them from vehicles and animals, and replace dead plants quickly. Treated waste water can sometimes be used for watering, if its quality and the permissions allow. Plan maintenance for at least the first three years. That is when most plants are lost.

What records should you keep?

Keep a planting map, a list of trees by type, survival counts, dated photos and maintenance logs. Good records make compliance reports quick, and they give you proof if the green belt is questioned during an inspection.

title: Building a School Cricket Ground That Drains After Rain
metaTitle: Building a Cricket Ground That Drains | Laavin
description: Building a school cricket ground that drains after rain: levelling, sub-surface drainage, Bermuda outfields, the pitch square and upkeep.
lead: A school ground takes more wear than almost any other grass: daily PE classes, inter-house matches, sports days and events, plus the monsoon. Whether a ground can be played on the morning after rain, or stays waterlogged for days, depends mostly on what is under the surface.
imageAlt: Cricket stumps on a grass pitch
body:
Step 1: How should the ground be levelled?

Start with a survey of the ground's levels. The design gives the surface a gentle, even slope, so water runs off instead of forming puddles. The slope stays slight enough for fair play. Levelling with laser-guided machines gives a much more even surface than levelling by eye.

Step 2: What drainage does a cricket ground need?

A slope alone cannot clear heavy monsoon rain. You also need drainage under the surface. Pipes with holes are laid in gravel-filled trenches, usually in a herringbone (V) pattern. They carry water to an outlet or a rainwater harvesting pit. On heavy clay soil, thin sand-filled cuts across the surface help water reach the drains faster.

Step 3: Which grass suits the outfield?

The outfield grass grows in a sandy layer laid over the drainage, which lets water pass through quickly. Bermuda grass, known locally as doob, is the most widely used grass for this in India. It handles heat and heavy use, and recovers quickly. It can be grown from small cuttings or laid as ready turf. It needs a few weeks to a few months to settle before the ground can be fully used.

Step 4: How is the pitch built?

The pitch is built separately from the outfield. It uses clay-rich soil, pressed down in layers, so it plays firm and even. It needs regular rolling, mowing and preparation before matches. Practice nets with artificial pitches take daily wear away from the main pitch.

Step 5: What about a running track?

A track around the ground needs a firm base, edging and its own drainage. The surface you choose, such as murram (red gravel), cinder or a synthetic surface, decides both the cost and how much upkeep the track needs.

Plan the work so the grass has fully settled before the school year starts. A ground opened too early gets damaged before the roots take hold.

Step 6: How is the ground kept in shape?

Sprinklers or pop-up sprinklers keep the outfield even through the dry months. A maintenance calendar should cover mowing, aerating, top dressing, feeding, weed control and rest periods after heavy use. Agree early who will look after the ground after handover.

Our work

We built a cricket ground, a multi-lane running track and the drainage under them for Angels Public School, Faridabad. See our sports ground services.

title: Drip Irrigation for Large Campuses: Where It Pays Off
metaTitle: Drip Irrigation for Large Campuses | Laavin Infrascapes
description: Where drip irrigation pays off on large campuses and highway plantations, how to zone and automate it, using STP water, and maintenance.
lead: Watering is one of the biggest running costs of a large landscape. On many Indian campuses it is still done with hoses or by flooding. Drip and automatic irrigation can cut that cost a lot, but only when the right system goes to the right part of the site.
imageAlt: Plant nursery with misting irrigation system
body:
How does drip irrigation work?

A drip system gives water slowly, through small outlets (emitters) placed at each plant's roots. Very little water is lost to evaporation or runoff, so far less is wasted than with hose or flood watering. Drip also keeps leaves and paths dry, which means less disease and fewer weeds.

Where does drip work best?

  • Shrub beds, hedges and ground cover.
  • Trees, including rows of roadside trees and median planting.
  • Terrace gardens, planters and green walls.

Where does drip not work?

Lawns and sports grounds need even water across the whole surface. Sprinklers or pop-up sprinklers on timers work better there. Most large campuses use both: drip for beds and trees, sprinklers for grass.

What is zoning, and why does it matter?

Zoning means grouping plants that need similar water, sun and soil. Each group (zone) gets its own valve and watering schedule. A shady shrub bed and a sunny lawn should never be watered on the same schedule. Good zoning is what makes an irrigation system actually save water.

Can irrigation run automatically?

Yes. A controller waters each zone on its own schedule, at times of day when less water evaporates. Rain or soil-moisture sensors can skip a watering after rain. Larger systems can be checked and changed remotely, which helps when the garden team is small.

Can drip use borewell or STP water?

Yes. City supply, borewells and treated sewage (STP) water can all feed a drip system. Treated water saves fresh water, but it carries particles that block emitters. So it needs good filters and regular flushing. Hard borewell water can leave scale in emitters and may need treatment from time to time.

Most drip systems fail because nobody looks after them, not because of bad design. Plan for filter cleaning, line flushing and emitter checks from the first month.

How do you maintain a drip system?

Clean the filters regularly, flush the pipes, check emitters for blockages, repair damage from mowing or digging, and change the schedules with the seasons. A system that is looked after keeps saving water for years.

What do we need to design your system?

  • Your site and planting plan.
  • Your water source, water pressure and water quality.
  • Details of any existing irrigation that could be reused.

See our irrigation services, and our guide to office landscaping for how irrigation fits into the wider design.
